On the British North West Africa Grid (tools/grid_ref.py nwa): lands about 8 km east of Ferryville, east of Lake Bizerte, against the June entry's 3 mi east (the offset). The square letter J: the lettering (repeated in each 500 km block) is fixed by AMS's 1942 Alger sheet's worked example (Mon Rouge = H743072; princeton-amsalger), which this J agrees with; previously inferred from this town check, not from a source. Check (28 Oct 2026, elevation tiles): both references fall on the south-east shore of Lake Bizerte, matching the June entry's "on east shore of Lake Bizerte", while 3 mi due east of the town is open water. A wrong square letter would put the point 100 km away, so this supports J.

Btry "C", 62d CA(AA). Every report from Aug 1943 to Apr 1944 gives this station: first forms of each month read on the scan, rg64-451686722/p0847 (Sep), rg64-454456048/p0571 (Oct), rg64-456824820/p0772 (Nov), rg64-459809807/p0660 (Dec), rg64-461617355/p0688 (2 Jan 1944), rg64-463957373/p0651 (Feb), rg64-466426100/p0339 (Mar); 4 Aug typed "Palermo, Italy" (p0048), a slip. August's records of events: "Battery went into action against enemy planes who dropped flares and attacked" (p0045); "Enemy planes flared and attacked Palermo harbor. One plane shot down" (p0073, page undated, about 22-23 Aug). Every record of events from Sep 1943 to Apr 1944 read on the scan (29 Oct 2026): "Usual field duties." on almost every day; alerts on 9 Nov 1943, 10 Feb 1944 and 27 Mar 1944 (actions.csv); practice: "preliminary target practice on Mt. Pelligrimo" 18 Oct 1943 (rg64-454456048/p0606), small arms on the I.B.S. range 25 Oct (p0620), field artillery practice at Mondello 10 Feb 1944 (rg64-463957373/p0671) and "at Mondello Beach" 16 Feb (p0684). 15 Oct 1943: a man of the battery shot and killed near the position by a soldier of another unit (rg64-454456048/p0600), not enemy action. "Battery "C", 62nd CA(AA) reorganized as Battery "C", 62d AAA Gun Bn." on 24 Mar 1944 (rg64-466426100/p0384; forms from p0382). No move recorded through 30 Apr (rg64-468998085/p0703).

January 1943 (cover p0044). As written: the transport USS Ancon, in convoy UGF-4. 1-10: Ft. Dix, usual camp duties. "10-20" is the report's ten-day block. The Regimental HQ Battery's report has the dates: left Fort Dix by rail at 0730 on 13 Jan, embarked on the Ancon at the New York Port of Embarkation, Staten Island, at 1600; sailed at 0530 on 14 Jan; reached Oran at 1800 on 26 Jan, 3800 miles by water (rg64-427223420/p0730).

The Ancon's war diary agrees (as summarised by the 32nd Station Hospital, which crossed on her), so the detachment's "26" is probably a day early. 27-31: usual camp duties.

station: Plane continued to Q-7831 grid and strafed Batteries "A" and "B" of 693rd F.A. Battalion at which time 2nd Platoon of "D" Battery ... engaged
note: January 1945 history: a P-51 with American markings strafing near Lichtenberg and Wimmenau went on to strafe the 693rd FA's batteries at Q-7831, and Battery D's 2nd Platoon engaged it. The only January entry that places any part of Battery D; it was defending the 45th Division Artillery Cub air field and the 189th FA Bn all month (p03). The same record says the battalion CP moved early in January from Merkweiller to Schillersdorf and then to La Petite Pierre, without dates (p07). Morning reports for 1945 aren't online.
General Orders No. 3, Hq 106th AAA AW Bn, 9 Feb 1945: the battalion reorganized under T/O & E 44-75 "at La Petite Pierre, France". Battalion headquarters; the batteries' positions aren't given.

17-18 Feb the battalion withdrew from the line with the 45th Inf Div into a rest area: "each Battery be located in a different village in the locality, with Battalion Headquarters at Rehaincourt (V-062744)". Battery D's village isn't named. Rest and training there until 12 Mar (March history, ok45th-17570/p04).

"This battalion convoyed with the 45th Infantry Division to Saarguemines (Q-539561), France. Mission was the protection of the convoy route for the Division installations." The journal (p20): the Forward Echelon left Rehaincourt at 1300A and set up the battalion CP at Q-539561 "in Alsace" at 1730A.

"The forward CP of this Battalion moved from its position by convoy and entered Germany. The Battalion CP was set up in Herbitzhein ... at 1700A." Herbitzheim in the Saarland (Gersheim), not the Alsace village of the same name: the grid falls there.
Battalion Forward Echelon left Herbitzhiem at 1415A; CP set up at 1600A. Mimbach (Blieskastel).
Battalion forward CP left Mimbach at 1200A, arrived 1500A. Typed "Homberg"; the next day's entry has HOMBURG (p31).
Forward CP moved at 1230A from HOMBURG, arrived 1545A. The grid as typed falls 54 km north of Eisenberg; M-242063 falls on it, so probably two digits transposed. Placed at the town.
The forward Echelon moved from Eisenberg and opened the CP at 1030A.
Forward battalion CP moved from Guntershiem at 1800A, set up CP 1940A. The grid falls 10 km north of the town (M-425225 would fall on it); placed at the town.

"The Battalion C.P. at 1320A leaving Osthofen, Germany and Crossing the Rhine River Arrived at Seehiem Germany and set up C.P. at 1800A." The March narrative (p07) has the battalion crossing the Rhine at Worms on 27 March (the town name is blurred). Seeheim(-Jugenheim), south of Darmstadt; the grid agrees.
Closed CP and the Battalion Forward CP moved to Mosbach, arriving 1830A. Mosbach in Hesse (Schaafheim), not Mosbach in Baden: the grid falls there.

station: positions of the 189th Field Artillery Bn area and the highway in the vicinity of M-977495

"It put on two firing demonstrations in the spring of 1944 while stationed at Camp Polk, La." (G.I. Stories booklet). Date approximate. The division had trained at Fort Riley (1942-43) and Camp Ibis in the Mojave (Jun-Oct 1943) before Louisiana; the 8th Armored was also at Camp Polk from late 1943.

station: New York (sailed on the Queen Mary)
note: Overseas 26 Aug 1944 (Wikipedia, from the Army's order of battle); "In August, 1944, the division sailed for England aboard the Queen Mary" (booklet). Route assumed.
"After drawing equipment in the Tidworth area, the 9th crossed the Channel" (booklet). Reached the UK in September 1944 (Wikipedia); date approximate. Arrived by sea (the Queen Mary).
"The 9th Armored Division landed in Normandy late in September 1944" (Wikipedia); then "a six-day march across France" (booklet). Where it landed isn't given.
Third Army's Provost Marshal, October 1944: "9th Armored Division (to Ninth U.S. Army) from VERDUN (U2865) to LONGUYON (U4596) via N64, N405, GC5, GC6 and N18" (read on the scan). No day given.
First into the line 23 Oct 1944 on the quiet Luxembourg-German frontier (Wikipedia). "Gen. Eisenhower and Gen. Bradley paid the division a visit at Mersch, Luxembourg, in November" (booklet).

station: Ardennes: CC B at St. Vith, CC A near Beaufort, CC R east of Bastogne
note: The German offensive found the division's three combat commands far apart: CC B at Faymonville, then St. Vith (until 21-23 Dec); CC A near Beaufort, Luxembourg; CC R blocking the roads east of Bastogne (booklet). Not mapped: the division's position stands for all three.

Company A, 2nd Tank Bn, 31 Dec 1944 (read on the scan); the battalion's headquarters company also reports Hagnicourt from 23 Dec. The division's command post was at Etalle, Belgium, from 23 Dec and at Guignicourt-sur-Vence (Ardennes) from 30 Dec, and the division went into SHAEF Reserve on 31 Dec (etoob-9AD/p503-504, p502). On 8 Jan it was taken out of the line to refit (aar3/p097).

"The 8th and 9th Armored Divisions moved to PONT A MOUSSON (U7735) and THIONVILLE (U8687) respectively, on 12 January" (Third Army Provost Marshal, January; read on the scan). Assigned to Fifteenth Army from 8 Jan and attached to Third Army from 9 Jan (etoob-9AD/p502); Third Army's Quartermaster Section says the 8th and 9th Armored Divisions "were attached to the Third U. S. Army for supply and administration on 11 January, but remained assigned to the Fifteenth U. S. Army" (aar3/p626, read on the scan), two days after the order of battle's date. The division's command post was at Bockange from 12 Jan, about 22 km from both Thionville and Metz, and at Ennery, between the two and about 12 km north of Metz, from 14 Jan (etoob-9AD/p503-504).

Figure 13, "Antiaircraft Situation 31 Jan 1945" (read on the scan, enlarged): inside the Metz gun-defense circle, the 9th Armored Division's symbol (a boxed XX 9) east of the city centre, with 482 (the 482nd AAA AW Bn) beside it; the 128th AAA Gun Bn's symbol on the west side. The same chapter says the 482nd was reattached to the 9th Armored Division when the division returned to the Third Army area on 11 January (aar3/p097, read on the scan), which fits the reading of that symbol; the 28 Feb map (aar3/p099, read on the scan) has no division symbol at Metz. What the map establishes: the division's symbol in the Metz defense area on 31 Jan. It is schematic: it places no command post or unit of the division on the ground, and doesn't say when the division arrived.

February: "9th Armored Division from METZ (U8557) to SPRIMONT (K5414)" (read on the scan). When it moved from Thionville to Metz isn't given; the date here is a placeholder. The 128th AAA Gun Bn was at Metz from about 20 January.

Command post at Sprimont (Liege), Belgium, from "22 Feb 45" (command posts, pp. 503-504: the web edition doesn't mark which). The same day the division was assigned to III Corps, First Army, and its attachment to Third Army ended (p502), and the 482nd AAA AW Bn (SP) and 656th TD Bn (SP) were attached (p500). Third Army's February movements give the move "from METZ (U8557) to SPRIMONT (K5414)" with no day (aar3/p558). The command post was at Gey, Germany, on 28 Feb (pp. 503-504).
CC B took the Ludendorff bridge at Remagen intact, 7 Mar 1945, after a dash through Euskirchen (booklet).
"CC B struck south along the river to Ehrenbreitstein, March 22"; the division moved from III to V Corps (booklet).
Photo caption: 9th Armored Division half-tracks advancing through Engers, 27 Mar 1945 (Wikipedia). Then Limburg and its prison camp, and the drive north to Fritzlar and the Ruhr pocket.
"CC B beat off a strong counter-attack near Bonenberg, April 2" (booklet; the village is Bonenburg, south of Warburg).

From 10 April the division raced "from Warburg to the Mulde River ... in carrying out the encirclement of Leipzig", which the 2nd and 69th Infantry Divisions took (booklet). Date approximate: Leipzig fell on 19-20 April.

Sent south to Third Army; "CC A advanced into Czechoslovakia with the 1st Inf. Div." and met Soviet troops near Karlsbad (booklet). Only one combat command; the rest of the division's position isn't given.

The Second Army's Tennessee Maneuver Area. Typed with "Nashville, Tennessee" above it, and on 4 Feb the other way round (p0380); placed at Nashville. When the battery left Fort Bliss isn't in the pages found (its January reports are at Fort Bliss).
Camp Forrest, at Tullahoma; placed at the town.
"SA Hq Btry": the staging area (SA) of the New York Port of Embarkation.
At sea. The ship isn't named.
An APO number only, in the UK; not on the map.
Handwritten. Camp Monmouth at Llanover Park, near Abergavenny, Wales; placed at Llanover. Arrived by sea (route assumed).
Marshalling for Normandy; Marabout Barracks is at Dorchester, Dorset. The battery's reports say Blandford until then.

At sea. A Battery B veteran remembered coming ashore at Omaha Beach on 28 June.
"DeLasse" isn't identified; the reference (Lambert Zone I) is about 10 km southeast of Cherbourg. Arrived by sea (LST).

Typed "U-½ 854103" (the same on 25 Sep, p1600, and "U-854103" later); read as U-854103. The battalion defended Nancy into January 1945.

station: Metz (gun defenses moved from Nancy and Toul)
note: Third Army AAR, Antiaircraft Section, January 1945: the supplies stored around Nancy and Toul had been depleted, so "Antiaircraft defenses at these two cities were therefore discontinued on 20 January and the units furnishing defense for these two points were moved to the city of METZ (U8858) which had become an important supply center" (read on the scan). The 128th is by Nancy on the 25 Dec situation map (p095) and by Metz on the 31 Jan map (p098).

Figure 14, "Antiaircraft Situation 28 Feb 1945": the 128th's 90 mm gun symbol just northwest of Metz, inside the Metz gun-defense circle (read on the scan). The battalion's symbol, not the headquarters battery's own position. The 9th Armored Division moved from Metz to Sprimont in February.

Figure 16: the 128th inside the gun-defense circle around the Rhine crossing at Boppard, south of Koblenz (read on the scan). VIII Corps crossed at Boppard on 25 March. A Battery B veteran recalled crossing the Rhine at Oppenheim and attending Easter Mass (1 April) near there (Robert Chouinard, Veterans History Project).

Figure 17: "128 2 BTRY" in a gun-defense circle just south of Grafenwöhr, and a small 128 symbol east of Nürnberg (read on the scan). In late April two of its batteries, "with a provisional Hq supervising", leapfrogged with the 11th Armored Division to protect its armor and CP (weekly AA reports, p144). Where the headquarters battery was isn't certain.

station: Plattling (battalion less one battery; Antiaircraft Situation 4 May 1945)
note: Figure 18: "128 (-) 1 BTRY" on the Isar near Plattling, a 128 symbol further east, north of Passau, and the small 128 symbol still near Nürnberg (read on the scan). The battalion less a battery is most likely to include headquarters. V-E Day was four days later; a Battery B veteran was in Austria.

station: in the immediate vicinity of Larochette (Fels), in central Luxembourg
note: "The 60th Armored Infantry Battalion completed the last leg of its journey across France on October 20 1944. Arriving at its targeted bivouac area in the immediate vicinity of Larochette (Fels), in central Luxembourg, at 1250." Then under Combat Command A, 9th Armored Division, in bivouac for the rest of the period. In the transcription this report has no month heading; its period is taken to be October.

station: in position relieving the 1/121 (8th Infantry Division), between the Our and Sauer Rivers
note: "The relief of the 1/121 was completed on Nov 2 1944 at 1050 with our troops in position." The sector is described by its terrain ("The Our River and the Sauer River ran between the two lines"; Bollendorf and Wallendorf, Germany, named as landmarks) but no village for the battalion is named, so no place is given. The battalion was in bivouac near Larochette before (the major portion of its transportation stayed there), and was relieved by the 1/121 on 9 Nov at 1230; where it went then is not stated (the report is headed "Day's location : 60-AIB, December 5 1944, Steinsel - Heisdorf, Luxembourg").

station: in tactical bivouac in vicinity of Larochette (Fels)
note: "From Dec 1 to Dec 9, the 60-AIB was assigned to CCA, 9-AD. ... Approximately half of the unit was in tactical bivouac in vicinity of Larochette (Fels), and the remainder in billets in and around Heisdorf." Position for the first half; the other half at Heisdorf.

station: a sector of the line assigned to 9-AD (relieving the 2/109)
note: "By Dec 10, at 1110, the battalion completed relieving the 2/109, in a sector of the line assigned to 9-AD." No place is named for the sector. On 16 Dec the report puts the German attack through the draws at Dilligen and Grundhof, with the front companies at Beaufort, Luxembourg, by 17 Dec.

station: Battalion Motor Park in the vicinity of Savelborn
note: "With the enemy in control of Beaufort ... at 1743, the Hq & Hq Co (minus) withdrew to the Battalion Motor Park in the vicinity of Savelborn." Headquarters company only; the rifle companies were cut off at Beaufort and the front line, and the report gives no single battalion position for them. Not mapped: the position is the headquarters company's, and no battalion position is given.
"The 60-AIB's CP was moved to 9136" (19 Dec), on the defensive line Waldbillig - Ermsdorf. A four-figure reference with no map sheet or place: not placed.

"At 1600, Dec 26, the 60-AIB was relieved in the Savelborn sector and as part of CCA, 9-AD, moved immediately to Longlier, Belgium. Arriving at 2345, CCA, was attached to the 4th Armored Division." The report writes "Dec 19" for the following day's attack (8 o'clock, along the Neufchateau - Bastogne road); the context makes it 27 Dec.

station: the high ground north of Sibret
note: Task Force Collins (the battalion less Baker Co, with attachments): "Upon taking Sibret our direction of advance was changed ... to secure the high ground north of Sibret which was accomplished by night fall, December 27." At darkness road blocks surrounded Sibret and Able Co occupied the high ground north of it.

station: the high ground south of the town (Chenogne)
note: 30 Dec: Task Force Collins took Chenogne; "At darkness our troops pulled back and occupied the high ground south of the town". Attacked from Chenogne on 31 Dec at 0530; Charlie Co fell back to a reserve position just north of Sibret and "By noon our troops had been reorganized and the line firmly established." No distance from the town is given.

station: the high ground immediately north of Sibret, Belgium
note: "From midnight to early morning, January 1 1945, Task Force Collins, as part of CCA-9-AD, held the high ground immediately north of Sibret, Belgium." It attacked at 1100 toward the high ground south of the railroad between Chenogne and Senonchamps and was "digging in on its objective" within five or six hours (no place named for it beyond that). CCA was relieved by the 17th Airborne Division on the afternoon of 3 Jan.

station: in the vicinity of Volaiville, Belgium
note: "Immediately the 60-AIB began its march to the rear, spending the night, January 4, in the vicinity of Volaiville, Belgium." The same report later has the march resuming "on the morning of January 4 from the vicinity of Volaiville", so its own dates disagree; the relief was on 3 Jan.

station: bivouac in and around the town of Veil-Saint-Rémy, between Rethel and Charleville-Méizières, France
note: "That night the 60-AIB closed into bivouac in and around the town of Veil-Saint-Rémy, between Rethel and Charleville-Méizières, France." The report puts the night at Volaiville on both 3 and 4 Jan, and the arrival here "that night" after leaving Volaiville on the 4th: so the 4th or the 5th. The date drawn is the 5th.

station: a bivouac area in and near Metzeresche, France
note: "The next, January 12, the march was resumed with the 60-AIB closing into a bivouac area in and near Metzeresche, France. We occupied this area during the reminder of January." Reconstituting supplies, reconditioning and receiving equipment, and intensive training. The division's command post was at Bockange, then Ennery (etoob-9AD/p503-504).

station: new billet areas near Trooz, Belgium
note: "At 0700, February 23, the 60-AIB, began marching from its billet areas in the vicinity of Metzeresche, France, to new billet areas near Trooz, Belgium, closing in the new areas at 2315 after a march of 186 miles." From 1 to 22 Feb the companies were "in billets in and near Metzeresche"; on 9 Feb Able Co (a company, not the battalion) moved from Mancy (Bettelainville) to Distroff, France, so no row for that. The battalion command post was at Trooz on 28 Feb.

station: assembly area in the village of Drove (Kreuzau), Germany
note: "The march began at 1215, with the battalion marching as part of CCA 9-AD, and at 2130 the battalion closed into its assembly area at Drove (Kreuzau), Germany." The commanding officer was placed in command of Task Force Collins at 2200, for an attack the next day.

station: marching in vehicles toward its objective, Wollersheim (Nideggen); the advance guard crossed the Line of Departure, Berg (Nideggen), at 0700
note: "Early morning, March 1, Task Force Collins began marching in vehicles toward its objective, Wollersheim (Nideggen), with the advance guard, Baker 60-AIB and 1 Plat 19-TB attached, crossing the Line of Departure, Berg (Nideggen), Germany, at 0700." Task Force Collins was the battalion less Charlie Co (with attachments). Only the advance guard (Baker Co) is placed at Berg; the report gives no position for the battalion as a whole that day (Able Co and Baker Co were pinned down near Wollersheim by night). Not mapped. The battalion had closed into Drove on 28 Feb.

station: in position west of Wollersheim (Nideggen), Germany
note: "After being cleared, the town was occupied for the night by Able Co and out posted on the high ground to the east by Charlie Co, while the remainder of the Task Force remained in position west of the town." The town was officially cleared at 1715 on 2 Mar. Task Force Collins, the battalion with attachments (Charlie Co 60-AIB joined it that morning). No distance from the town is given.

station: Wollersheim (Nideggen), Germany: Task Force Collins less Charlie Co
note: "When Charlie Co ( ) began its move, the remainder of Task Force Collins occupied Wollerscheim." Charlie Co moved east and occupied Langendorf at 0845 (a company, not the battalion, so no row for Langendorf). The Task Force stayed at Wollersheim until its move on 4 Mar.

station: moving at noon to the Line of Departure, Oberelvenich (Zülpich) to Nemmenich (Zülpich), to attack Euskirchen
note: "At noon, March 4, the Task Force, in column, began its move toward a Line of Departue, Oberelvenich (Zülpich) to Nemmenich (Zülpich), with the mission of clearing the north edge of Euskirchen and seizing a crossing on the Erft River in its zone of action." The attack was then launched with Able and Charlie Cos abreast; the report gives no battalion position other than this line, which is a line, not a place. Not mapped. The bridge over the Erft in Euskirchen had been blown when the Task Force arrived that day.

station: Euskirchen, Germany (its portion of the town), with a bridgehead over the Erft
note: "On March 5, Task Force Collins finished and occupied its portion of Euskirchen and maintained the bridgehead while constructed a crossing over the Erft River." Able and Charlie Cos had established the bridgehead at 0500; at 2145 Charlie Co attacked across the Erft toward Palmersheim (a company, so no row).

station: Odendorf, Germany: Task Force Collins less Charlie Co 60-AIB, closing at 0755
note: "On the morning of March 6, the Task Force less Charlie 60-AIB and the 1st Plat of Able 19-TB, moved from Euskirchen to Odendorf, closing at 0755 where it received orders to continue the attack of CCA-9-AD passing through friendly units at Rheinbach as soon as that town had been cleared." It crossed the Line of Departure in Rheinbach at 1300; the advance guard took Wormersdorf (2100) and Charlie Co Ersdorf (2220), companies, so no rows for them.

station: Lantershofen, Germany (the balance of the Task Force closed in at 0205)
note: "At this point, Task Force Collins halted with Baker and Charlie Cos occupying defensive positions on the high ground just east of the town, and the balance of the Task Force closed into Lantershofen." Baker Co passed through Charlie Co at Lantershofen at 0205. A PW collection point and the battalion CP were there; Able Co relieved Charlie Co in its defensive sector at 1535 on 7 Mar. The Task Force had halted "early the next morning" (7 Mar) after the night march from Odendorf.

station: Sinzig, Germany: the Task Force moved in at 0645; Able and Charlie Cos on the high ground south of the town
note: "On March 8, at 0645, the Task Force moved into Sinzig and by noon Able and Charlie 60-AIB occupied defensive positions on the high ground south of the town." Mission: protecting the Remagen Bridgehead in a sector west of the Rhine. The battalion was relieved from defensive positions by the 23-IR (2-ID) on 9 Mar afternoon, took a new sector on the west bank (Able Co, 0400, 10 Mar), was relieved again on 11 Mar and put on alert. "During the period March 8-12, when the companies were not defending a sector in the vicinity of Sinzig, their time was consumed in receiving, processing and training reinforcement": the battalion stayed at Sinzig until 12 Mar.

station: crossing the Rhine on a pontoon bridge in the vicinity of Kripp, about 2000 meters southeast of the Ludendorff bridge
note: "Effective March 12, 1800, the 60-AIB was attached to CCB-9-AD. Immediately orders were received to move the battalion to the vicinity of Unkel, and at 2025, the battalion began marching from Sinzig closing in its new assembly area at 2315. During this march the battalion crossed the Rhine River, using a pontoon bridge constructed by US Army Engineers in the vicinity of Kripp, approximately 2000 meters southeast of the main Ludendorff bridge in Remagen." The crossing was between 2025 and 2315; the time is not given.

station: assembly area east of the Rhine, in the vicinity of Unkel (closed in at 2315)
note: "Immediately orders were received to move the battalion to the vicinity of Unkel, and at 2025, the battalion began marching from Sinzig closing in its new assembly area at 2315." The report does not say the assembly area was in Unkel itself: it names the vicinity of Unkel as the destination, so this row is at the town only to that extent. "Upon closing into its first assembly area east of the Rhine River, the 60-AIB was attached to the 311-IR (78-ID)." It was then ordered to Rheinbreitbach "for a short time" on 13 Mar (arrival not stated), then to Bad Honnef.

station: Bad Honnef, Germany: securing the town, a defensive sector near its northeastern edge
note: "On March 13, the battalion was ordered to Rheinbreitbach, for a short time and then to Bad Honnef where it was assigned the mission of securing the town which had been taken by another unit that day." Defensive sector near the northeastern edge of the town; "At 1700 all companies were ordered back into town and established a system of road blocks." On 14-15 Mar the three rifle companies attacked separate hill objectives north and east of Bad Honnef (Objectives #14, #15, #16, #17, Perlenhardt, Margarethenhof): company positions, so no battalion row for them.

station: attacking Ittenbach from Objective #16 (Able and Charlie Cos abreast; Baker Co in battalion reserve)
note: "Able and Charlie Cos abreast jumped off at 0910 ... Baker Co was then ordered to occupy Objective #16 as battalion reserve." Able Co gained "that portion of the city west of the creek" by 1515; Charlie Co was held out of its objective that night and the German commander surrendered the town to Charlie Co at about 1000-1200 on 17 Mar. The report puts no battalion command post in Ittenbach, but "Upon leaving Ittenbach the battalion marched to Bad Honnef", so the battalion was there when it was relieved (1900, by the 2/310-IR, 78-ID, on the night after the surrender, 17 Mar). Placed at the town on the strength of that sentence; Objective #16 (Margarethenhof) is not placed.

station: Bad Honnef, Germany: the battalion closed in at 2330 on its march from Ittenbach
note: "Upon leaving Ittenbach the battalion marched to Bad Honnef closing in at 2330. There it received orders to move to the vicinity of Linz the next morning at 0700 and over the same route used in its march to Bad Honnef." Relieved from attachment to the 311-IR (78-ID) at 1900 and reverted to CCB-9-AD.

station: the vicinity of Linz, Germany (the movement completed on 18 Mar)
note: "This movement was completed on March 18 at 111." (The hour is as transcribed, evidently a typing error.) "During the period March 18-21, the battalion was out of contact with the enemy": maintenance, reinforcements, a few men sent to Paris on 3 day passes. Attached to CCA-9-AD in place on 19 Mar at 2400; back under CCB on 21 Mar at 1200.

station: assembly area in the vicinity of Hammerstein, Germany (closed in at 0350)
note: "Receiving orders during the night of March 21 to move to an assembly area in the vicinity of Hammerstein in preparation for an attack early the next morning. The battalion moved at 0230 closing into its assigned area at 0350." The three rifle companies then moved dismounted at 0600 toward the Wied River, and Charlie Co crossed it at 1830 on a foot bridge (the river crossing is not placed to a village in the report). On 23-24 Mar the companies advanced in short moves; the report names no place for the battalion again until Bendorf on 25 Mar.

station: Bendorf, Germany: Baker, Able and Charlie Cos crossed the Saynbach and entered the town (1110)

At 0400, Able Co reported all AA guns destroyed and the 60-AIB's final objective occupied." The final objective was the high ground (the Mallendarer Berg). Relieved in place by the 27-AIB by noon on 26 Mar; no battalion command post is named, so the place is the town the companies cleared.

station: the west bank of the Lahn River opposite Diez, Germany (reached at 1950)

Reaching the west bank of the Lahn at 1950 without opposition, the 60-AIB met there its first resistance from a group of stubborn enemy dug in on the east bank of the river." All bridges were blown. Mapped at the town of Diez, but the battalion was on the bank opposite it (the report places the enemy on the east bank).

station: in and around Diez, Germany, Able and Baker Cos in defensive positions around the town
note: "Able and Baker Cos then took up defensive positions around the town." Able Co crossed the Lahn at the south edge of Diez on a barge and cleared the town; Baker and Charlie Cos had been sent north to the vicinity of Limburg. "The battalion remained in position until 1115, March 28, when it was relieved in place by the 2nd Ranger Battalion." All movement orders were cancelled for 24 hours at mid-afternoon on 27 Mar.

station: Hofen (Runkel), Germany: the battalion less Charlie Co closed in at 2000
note: "At 1400, CCA began moving to the new assembly area with the 60-AIB less Charlie Co marching near the end of the column behind seven other units. ... At 2000, the battalion closed into Hofen and immediately set up road blocks and a system of all-round security for the night." Charlie Co was attached to CCA and sent to Aumenau to relieve elements of CCB-9-AD protecting a Lahn bridgehead (a company, so no row for Aumenau). The report says only "Hofen"; the assembly area was to be in the vicinity of Hofen (Runkel).

No district or county is given for Oberhausen, and several places bear the name; none could be matched to this march with confidence, so the row is in the log and not on the map.

station: within 3000 meters of Fritzlar by 1330; the battalion in the attack on the town and its airfield
